Annales Veteris Testamenti

Annales Veteris Testamenti, a Prima Mundi Origine Deducti ('Annals of the Old Testament, Deduced from the First Origins of the World') is a 1650 work by Archbishop James Ussher of Armagh, representing the most comprehensive biblical chronology ever attempted. Drawing on the Hebrew Bible, Septuagint, and other ancient sources, Ussher's work provides a detailed timeline of human history from creation to the late 17th century. The chronology is based on a complex system of dating methods, including the biblical account of the Great Flood and the calculation of the solar year.

Ussher's work was groundbreaking because it attempted to reconcile seemingly contradictory biblical accounts and provide a coherent narrative of human history. The Annals also contain detailed information on the geography, politics, and culture of ancient civilizations, making it a valuable resource for historians and scholars.

The significance of Annales Veteris Testamenti lies in its impact on the development of biblical scholarship and historical chronology. Ussher's work influenced subsequent biblical scholars and historians, and its ideas continue to shape our understanding of ancient history.

In the words of Ussher himself, 'The Annals of the Old Testament are a most satisfactory exposition of the history of the world from the creation to the present time.'
